title: The One Problem With Star Wars, According to Andy Weir
summary:
Everyone has an opinion about Star Wars, including science-fiction author Andy Weir, who wrote "The Martian" and "Project Hail Mary." In a recent conversation, he shared what he would do if he were in charge of Star Wars.

His main concern is massive upheaval. "Star Wars is more about massive upheaval," he said. "One problem that happens is, if you're going to have a story about a monumental war, then when it's over and the good guys win, you want it to stay that way. So it's very unsatisfying if you roll into a new monumental war."

That criticism will sound familiar to fans of "The Force Awakens" from 2015: some viewers were uneasy that the original heroes' victory seemed undone, with the Empire and Rebellion effectively replaced by the First Order and Resistance.

Weir's suggestion looks back to "Rogue One," from nearly a decade ago. "I feel like the best way, in my opinion, to do another Star Wars movie," he said, "would be to have the story of other people during the Galactic Civil War." Luke Skywalker, Leia Organa and Han Solo were the movers and shakers of "A New Hope" and beyond, he acknowledged, but there is room for smaller, tangential stories alongside theirs.

"Think of it like this: We know what happened in World War II, but there are some really good fictional stories that take place during World War II," he said. "So if you treat the Galactic Civil War as established canon, there's still a lot of stories to tell about other people living through those wars."

Weir also praised "Andor," the Disney+ prequel series from Tony Gilroy, calling it amazing and really good, but said a series was the correct choice: a movie must tell its whole story in about two hours, while "Andor" was intellectual and clever.
why_it_matters: How a story handles victory shapes whether fans trust it, and Weir's idea shows that small stories inside a big war can matter as much as the main heroes'.
